b: We tend to think of dementia as a disease of memory. The forgotten name, the misplaced keys, the story told twice in the same afternoon. Memory loss is typically what brings people to the doctor, and it’s one of the most noticeable and debilitating symptoms associated with dementias’ gradual decline. But that framing, focusing on memory loss alone, is incomplete.

The brain is not a sealed processor siloed away from the rest of the world. It is an input-dependent organ evolved to produce cognitive and behavioral outputs—its job is to understand and interact with the environment around us. It is constantly building and revising a model of its surroundings from a stream of sensory information: what we hear, what we see, where our body is in space, which way is up or down, what is currently occurring within our body. Every conversation, every unfamiliar street, every uneven trail is a constant stream of data used by the brain to test its predictions and update its model.

As we age, that stream degrades. Our senses can dull with time. The world gets quieter, dimmer. And when the input degrades, the behavior that depends on it—and the neurological machinery running underneath it all—changes too.

Consider what happens downstream of each sensory impairment. A person with untreated hearing loss starts skipping the dinner party because following conversations in a noisy restaurant is exhausting, if not outright futile. A person with cataracts stops driving at night. Then they stop driving to the next town. A person whose balance is slipping avoids stairs, crowds, gravel paths, and travel. A person with neuropathy in their hands stops playing music. With neuropathy in their feet, they walk less, as they may no longer trust the ground.

Each of these is a small, rational adjustment. Together, they produce a smaller life: fewer conversations, less novelty, less navigation, less movement, less environmental complexity. The brain’s job is to experience the world around us—and when it stops doing so, it loses access to the fundamental processes that keep it healthy and functioning.

This observation is broadly referred to as the shrinking world hypothesis. Now, it is a hypothesis—it is difficult to prove entirely, and it’s certainly an incomplete picture of dementia development. It doesn’t tell us about amyloid, pTau, or alpha synuclein pathology. Nonetheless, it is useful: it takes a step back from molecular biology, and helps organize what would otherwise be a scattered literature spanning across hearing, vision, balance, and signals from inside the body, and how they each influence dementia risk.

The Lancet Commission’s 2024 report identified that as many as 45% of dementia cases could be prevented through modifiable risk factors: 9% coming from hearing or vision loss, and 7% from physical inactivity and social isolation. This means that, of the dementia cases that their model predicts we could potentially avoid through lifestyle and medical interventions, 20% were related to sensory loss, and another 15% came from behaviors related to a shrinking world.1

This positions sensory loss—and the prevention and treatment of sensory impairment—as one of the few niches of dementia literature that is useful for people alive today. It points towards things we can actually do.

What we’ll do here is lay out a framework for how we should understand the literature available—how does losing a sense actually contribute to dementia development? We’ll walk through the evidence for four systems—hearing, sight, balance and proprioception, and even early evidence for interoception, and dive into the mechanisms through which they appear to contribute to disease. And having seen how these sensory systems correlate with dementia risk, we’ll lay out the steps we each should take to protect—or even revitalize—our senses.
